key_facts: **Spitz naevi** are benign naevi of large epithelioid/spindle melanocytes that **grow quickly in children**.
Pink-red or pigmented dome; dermoscopy starburst pattern or dotted vessels. **Reed naevus**: dark symmetrical starburst, often thigh of young women.
They can be clinically and histologically hard to tell from melanoma (spitzoid melanoma).
Children under 12 with typical lesions may be monitored by specialists; **adolescents and adults: excision**.
Atypical Spitz tumours need specialist histopathology review.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: A **Spitz naevus** is a benign naevus made of large epithelioid and/or spindle melanocytes, typically a fast-growing pink or pigmented dome in a **child**. A **Reed naevus** (pigmented spindle cell naevus) is a dark, symmetrical variant, often on the thigh of young women.

sub: Mostly children and young adults; face and limbs.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: Driven by HRAS mutations or kinase fusions (ALK, ROS1, NTRK and others); growth is followed by stabilisation. **Atypical Spitz tumours** lie between benign Spitz naevi and spitzoid melanoma.

ul: **"Fast growth always means melanoma"**: in young children it is typical of Spitz naevi, but needs specialist assessment.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Spitz naevi grow from a **single driver event** (HRAS mutation or kinase fusion), then stop.

mech.t: An HRAS mutation or a kinase fusion (ALK, ROS1, NTRK, BRAF, MET) starts growth.
Large epithelioid and spindle melanocytes proliferate over months.
Senescence halts growth; many involute or become fibrotic over years.
Additional mutations push lesions towards atypical Spitz tumour and spitzoid melanoma.

histo: Symmetrical, well-circumscribed proliferation of large epithelioid/spindle melanocytes with Kamino bodies; maturation with depth.

ul: **Spitz**: pink-red or pigmented, dome-shaped, smooth, rapidly growing over months in a child; face and limbs. Dermoscopy: starburst or dotted vessels.
**Reed**: black, symmetrical, starburst pattern; thigh in young women.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Dermoscopy plus age and growth pattern. Excision for histology in adolescents and adults, and in any atypical lesion; specialist histopathology review.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses
blocks: **Spitzoid melanoma** (adults, asymmetry), pyogenic granuloma, juvenile xanthogranuloma, haemangioma, dermatofibroma, nodular melanoma.

ul: Children under 12 with a typical lesion: specialist may monitor with dermoscopy.
**Adolescents/adults: excision** (atypical Spitz tumour and spitzoid melanoma differential).
Reed naevi are usually excised for histology.

ladder.t: Dermatology via the suspected cancer pathway; excision for histology.

refer.t: Spitz-like lesion in an adolescent or adult; any atypical features.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: A Spitz-like lesion in an adult, or any atypical, ulcerated or rapidly growing lesion: **suspected cancer pathway**.
Diagnostic uncertainty; rarely malignant behaviour (atypical Spitz tumour).
Benign in most children; may regress.

pearls: Rapid growth worries parents but is typical of Spitz naevi in children; age decides how worried to be.

quiz.q: Typical patient with a Spitz naevus?
quiz.a: A child with a fast-growing pink dome.
A pigmented spindle-cell naevus: dark symmetrical starburst, often on a young woman's thigh.
